title: Re'eh: open thy hand (Deuteronomy 15:7–8)
hook: don't harden your heart or shut your hand; "thou shalt surely open thy hand"

segments.voice: Yesterday, re'eh: see the fork in the road, this day. Your line was see the choice. Did you catch yours? Today, a choice that comes up every time someone asks you for help. Day four hundred ninety-eight.

A man is standing at the light with a cardboard sign. You see him from three cars back. And in the seconds before you reach him, a whole conversation can start up inside. Do I have cash? Will he spend it well? Is it safe to roll the window down? The light's about to change anyway. Sometimes, by the time the thinking is done, the moment's gone. The Torah knows that inner conversation, and it names the two body parts where it happens: the heart, and the hand.
screen: `A SIGN AT THE LIGHT.` → `THE CONVERSATION INSIDE.` → `THE HEART, AND THE HAND.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish translation: "thou shalt not harden thy heart, nor shut thy hand from thy needy brother; but thou shalt surely open thy hand unto him." Notice the order. The heart hardens first, then the hand closes. Giving starts inside, before any money moves. And notice the doubling. Surely open thy hand is, in Hebrew, patoach tiftach: open, you shall open. The rabbis read the double verb as open, and open again. Not once. The verse goes on: lend him sufficient for his need. His need, not your idea of his need. The word for all of this in Jewish life is today's word, tzedakah. It's often translated charity, but it shares a root with tzedek, justice, righteousness. Charity sounds like something extra you choose to do when you feel generous. Tzedakah is closer to what's right, what's owed, part of how a just society works. And how you give matters too. We met Maimonides' eight levels of tzedakah earlier in the year; here's their shape again. Giving grudgingly is the lowest. Giving before you're asked is higher. Giving so neither side knows the other is higher still. And the highest of all: helping someone with a loan, a partnership or a job, so they won't need to ask again. A few verses later the Torah says plainly that there will always be poor people in the land. That's not a shrug. It's the reason the hand must keep opening.
screen: `THE HEART HARDENS, THE HAND CLOSES.` · `PATOACH TIFTACH: OPEN, AND OPEN.` · `TZEDAKAH, FROM TZEDEK: JUSTICE.` · `EIGHT LEVELS, A JOB AT THE TOP.` · then, large: `OPEN THY HAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give without hesitating. Settle, and breathe. Make two fists, and notice how they feel. Tight, ready, closed. Now slowly open them, palms up, resting on your knees. Stay like that. Think of the last time someone asked you for help and you hesitated. What was the conversation inside you? You don't have to judge it. Just notice it, palms open. Then decide on one gift you'll give today, quickly, before the conversation starts. The bell holds the time.
Tzedakah. Giving to those in need, from tzedek, justice. Not an extra, but part of what's right.
Your line: open thy hand. Today, when someone asks, give before your heart has time to harden. Small is fine. Day four hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Some Jewish homes keep a tzedakah box, called a pushke, and drop coins in before the Sabbath; a tenth of income is a common measure, and Maimonides' eight levels are still taught.

fork.setup: you want to give at the highest of Maimonides' eight levels. what do you do?
options: give a large gift with your name on it.
help someone with a loan, a partnership or a job.
fork.reveal: the top level strengthens someone so they won't need to ask again.

original.note: Hebrew: righteous giving, from tzedek, justice. often translated charity.

trapdoor: what you thought: tzedakah means charity.
what it means: giving as justice, with an open heart first, sized to the other person's real need.
what a scholar hears: patoach tiftach, the doubled verb; Maimonides' eight levels in the Laws of Gifts to the Poor, chapter ten.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook and practice no longer tell the listener what happens inside them; 'the great' dropped from Maimonides and the eight levels named as a callback to day 424; 'Jewish law sets a tenth' corrected to 'a common measure' (codes give a tenth to a fifth); 'many homes' and 'widely taught' softened.
Deuteronomy 15:7–8 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify.
Rabbinic reading of patoach tiftach as giving even many times (Sifrei; Bava Metzia 31a on doubled verbs); confirm source.
Maimonides' eight levels: Laws of Gifts to the Poor 10:7–14; the order of intermediate levels simplified in the script.
Tithing a tenth (ma'aser kesafim) as a common measure; customs and rulings vary.
